'''Root Cause Analysis Solver Engine''' (informally '''RCASE''') is a proprietary [[algorithm]] developed from research originally at the [[Warwick Manufacturing Group|Warwick Manufacturing Group (WMG)]] at [[Warwick University]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Overview of Warwick Analytical Software Limited|url=http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/private/snapshot.asp?privcapId=244987022|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141108190609/http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/private/snapshot.asp?privcapId=244987022|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 8, 2014|publisher=[[Business Week]]|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Manufacturing Global, Emerging Predictive Analytics for the Manufacturing Industries|url=http://issuu.com/manufacturingglobal/docs/manufacturing_global_-_november_201/23?e=12487208/9845812|publisher=[[Issuu]]|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref> RCASE development commenced in 2003 to provide an automated version of [[root cause analysis]], the method of problem solving that tries to identify the root causes of faults or problems.<ref>{{cite news|title=When Academia Meets The Real World, The Experience Can Be Life-altering: A First Person Perspective by Dan Sommers, Warwick Analytics|url=http://blogs.technet.com/b/bizspark_featured_startups/archive/2014/02/27/when-academia-meets-the-real-world-the-experience-can-be-life-altering-a-first-person-perspective-by-dan-sommers-warwick-analytics.aspx|accessdate=8 November 2014|publisher=TechNet}}</ref> RCASE is now owned by the spin-out company Warwick Analytics where it is being applied to automated predictive analytics software.

==Algorithm==
The algorithm has been built from the ground up to be particularly suitable for the following situations:
* [[Dirty data|'dirty' data]]
* incomplete data
* big data
* small datasets
* complex problems for example multi-modal failure or with more than one solution
RCASE is considered to be an innovator in the field of [[Predictive analytics]] and falls within the category of ''[[Pattern recognition#Classification algorithms .28supervised algorithms predicting categorical labels.29|classification algorithms]]''. Because it was built to handle the data types above, it has been proven to have many advantages over other types of classification algorithms and [[Machine learning#Software|machine learning]] algorithms such as [[decision trees]], [[Artificial neural network|neural networks]] and [[Regression analysis|regression techniques]]. It does not require [[hypotheses]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Manufacturing 4.0 – From Industrialisation to Data-Driven Product Lifecycle|url=http://citizentekk.com/2013/11/05/manufacturing-4-0-industrialisation-data-driven-product-lifecycle/|publisher=Citizen Tekk|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref>

It has since been commercialised and made available for operating systems such as [[SAP SE|SAP]],<ref>{{cite web|title=SAP to boost growth opportunities, deliver innovation with disruptive solutions from partner tie-ups|url=http://www.informationweek.in/informationweek/news-analysis/277234/sap-boost-growth-opportunities-deliver-innovation-disruptive-solutions-partner-tie-ups|publisher=[[InformationWeek]]|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref> [[Teradata]] and [[Microsoft]].<ref>{{cite web|title=SAP Spurs Innovation by Powering More Than 500 Startups Globally With SAP HANA|url=http://www.news-sap.com/sap-spurs-innovation-by-powering-more-than-500-startups-globally-with-sap-hana/|publisher=[[SAP SE]]|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref> RCASE originated from manufacturing and is widely used in applications such as [[Six Sigma]], [[quality control]] and [[engineering]], [[product design]] and warranty issues. However it is also used in other industries such as [[e-commerce]], [[financial services]] and utilities where root cause analysis is required.<ref>{{cite news|title=How German-based SAP is creating a startup ecosystem from Silicon Valley|url=http://pando.com/2013/07/19/how-german-based-sap-is-creating-a-startup-ecosystem-from-silicon-valley/|accessdate=8 November 2014|publisher=[[Pando Daily]]}}</ref>

==Mechanism & architecture==
RCASE is non-statistical and thus does not require any [[hypotheses]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Analytical software could solve mass product recall problems|url=http://eandt.theiet.org/news/2010/oct/warwick-analytics.cfm|accessdate=8 November 2014|publisher=[[Engineering and Technology Magazine]]}}</ref> If the key parameters causing the issue or fault in a process are not present in a [[dataset]], it will still narrow the search space and advise where the root cause may lie. This is a different approach to statistical theories which try to find a [[best fit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Warwick Analytics pioneers manufacturing fault finder software|url=http://www.theengineer.co.uk/channels/production-engineering/software/warwick-analytics-pioneers-manufacturing-fault-finder-software/1007594.article|publisher=[[The Engineer (UK magazine)|The Engineer]]|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref>

RCASE is based on optimised combinatorial theory and runs on either a grid cluster or a [[High-performance computing|high performance]] [[in-memory database]]. The software will interface with all [[Manufacturing execution system|MES]] and [[Enterprise resource planning|ERP]] systems.<ref>{{cite web|title=Press release: Midlands Company could solve mass vehicle recall problems|url=http://www2.warwick.ac.uk/newsandevents/pressreleases/midlands_company_could/|publisher=University of Warwick|date=25 October 2010}}</ref> The result is a security system monitoring and preventing defective products from being produced. The output from the analysis will be markers that identify either an exact root cause of failure or a parametric region pointing high probability of failure (i.e. data-driven guidance on where to look next to gather data and resolve the root cause exactly).<ref name=ebr>{{cite web|title=Using Big Data to Achieve Zero Defects|url=http://www.businessrevieweurope.eu/magazines/14442|publisher=European Business Review|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref>

The software can be installed on Linux or Microsoft operating systems and deployed as [[On-premises software|On-Premises]] or [[Software as a service|Software-as-a-Service]] (“SaaS” or “cloud”).<ref>{{cite web|title=Warwick Analytics Revolutionises Manufacturing Processes at DEMO Fall 2013|url=http://finance.boston.com/boston/news/read/25388103/Warwick_Analytics_Revolutionises_Manufacturing_Processes_at_DEMO_Fall_2013_|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141108203740/http://finance.boston.com/boston/news/read/25388103/Warwick_Analytics_Revolutionises_Manufacturing_Processes_at_DEMO_Fall_2013_|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 8, 2014|publisher=[[Boston.com]]|accessdate=8 November 2014}}</ref>
